stem: A team preparing to launch an assistant sets its content-safety target as a hard 0% policy-violation rate, graded by a model classifier over a rolling window of 10,000 conversations, ahead of trust-and-safety sign-off. What threshold should the team set?

opts.t: Keep the target at a literal 0% policy-violation rate and treat any single violation as a launch-blocking failure.
Enforce the 0% target with a deterministic pattern check against the model's raw output text.
Drop the numeric threshold and have the trust-and-safety lead review flagged conversations weekly instead.
Re-anchor the bar to a small achievable non-zero rate, such as under 0.1% of the sampled window.

whyRight: An open-ended, model-graded property cannot sustain a hard zero — one miss makes the bar non-binding and future violations go unflagged. Re-anchoring to a small, deliberately achievable non-zero rate, set before results are seen, keeps the threshold a real gate rather than an aspiration nobody enforces.

whyWrong.A: A literal 0% target on an open-ended, model-judged property becomes non-binding the first time any violation occurs, since the bar cannot be sustained.
whyWrong.B: The property is model-graded, not deterministic; no pattern or field scan can decide whether free-text output is policy-violating.
whyWrong.C: Removing the numeric threshold entirely leaves no gate at all, and weekly qualitative review cannot substitute for a measured, agreed-in-advance rate.

t1Clause: graded by a model classifier — invert to a deterministic exact-match scan for a specific forbidden token, making the property code-checkable
lessonKey: 0 000 1 10 anchor e g non rate re small zero

stem: A RAG assistant's single overall quality metric drops twelve points, and the team must isolate which layer caused it before the release manager will approve the next deploy. Applying the two-layer evaluation principle, what should the team do?

opts.t: Refine the rubric used to compute the single overall quality score.
Move the pipeline to a higher-capability generation model to raise the overall score.
Read the retrieval and generation bars already tracked separately, and treat retrieval as the likely fault.
Split the score into a retrieval row (Recall@k) and a generation row (faithfulness), each cleared against its own bar.

whyRight: A blended score cannot say which layer moved. Splitting into a retrieval row measured against gold passage ids and a generation row measured for faithfulness isolates the regression to the layer that actually failed, since each layer must clear its own bar independently.

whyWrong.A: A better rubric still scores one blended number, so it still cannot attribute a regression to retrieval or to generation specifically.
whyWrong.B: A higher-capability model was never shown to be at fault, and it can produce more fluent answers over the same broken passages.
whyWrong.C: The stem states there is only a single blended score; separate retrieval and generation bars do not yet exist to read.

t1Clause: one overall quality metric, regression cannot be located — invert to the retrieval and generation bars already being tracked separately at 0.55 and 0.97

stem: A support assistant's accuracy drops the same week a prompt change ships to production handling 50,000 tickets weekly. Investigation shows the drop correlates with a simultaneous data-schema change, not the prompt. What should the team do before the on-call lead signs off?

opts.t: Roll back the prompt change immediately and monitor the quality dashboard for further drops.
Run the regression set and a controlled A/B against the prompt change, since it shipped right before the drop.
Re-run the regression set and a controlled A/B investigation against the data-schema change rather than the prompt edit.
Escalate to a higher-capability model, since the current model may no longer handle the task reliably.

whyRight: The timing coincidence points at the prompt, but the stated evidence points at the data-schema change instead. Attribution requires isolating the actual variable that moved, so the regression set and a controlled A/B must be re-run against the schema change, not the unrelated prompt edit.

whyWrong.A: Rolling back the prompt does nothing if the schema change is the actual cause, and dashboard monitoring only catches damage after users absorb it.
whyWrong.B: The stem already states the drop correlates with the schema change, not the prompt; testing the prompt again investigates a variable the evidence already clears.
whyWrong.D: Nothing in the evidence implicates the model itself, and a bigger model would not fix answers built on a broken upstream schema.

t1Clause: correlates with a simultaneous data-schema change, not the prompt — invert so the drop instead correlates specifically with the prompt change, with no schema change involved
lessonKey: against b change controlled data edit investigation prompt rather re regression run schema set than

stem: An agent handles single-step lookups correctly but fails broadly on tasks needing three or more reasoning steps. Retrieval Recall@k is verified at 0.94 and the prompt has passed clean review. What does this pattern indicate before the team funds further prompt rewrites?

opts.t: Retrieval is still the likely fault, so Recall@k should be re-measured before any other conclusion is drawn.
The prompt still contains ambiguous wording and needs a further rewrite, despite passing review.
Model mismatch: the model's reasoning capability is insufficient for this task, since every upstream layer is already cleared.
The application is failing to resend conversation history, causing context loss across turns.

whyRight: Retrieval and prompt are the cheaper, earlier layers and both have already cleared, which is precisely the signature the diagnosis order reserves for model mismatch: a broad failure on genuinely multi-step reasoning after every upstream layer is confirmed clean.

whyWrong.A: The stem already states Recall@k is verified at 0.94, so retrieval has already cleared and cannot be the fault.
whyWrong.B: The prompt already passed clean review; another rewrite patches a layer that was never implicated in the failure.
whyWrong.D: Lost conversation history explains forgotten facts across turns, not a broad multi-step reasoning failure verified against clean retrieval and prompt.

t1Clause: Retrieval Recall@k is verified at 0.94 — invert to Recall@k measured low (e.g. 0.55), leaving retrieval unverified

stem: A regulated support system sends an identical, compliance-mandated preamble on every request. Both p95 latency and monthly token cost exceed target, and the platform lead must approve the fix before next quarter's budget review. Select two appropriate actions.

opts.t: Cut the preamble by 60% to only the sections used most often.
Reorder the prompt so the static preamble comes first and enable prompt caching.
Add a model call at request time to summarize the preamble before sending it.
Decline the proposal to cut the preamble, since the removed sections are compliance-mandated.

whyRight: Reordering for a stable prefix and enabling caching reuses the same required content at a fraction of the cost and latency, while declining the cut preserves compliance-mandated sections a proposed 60% reduction would remove — both actions preserve everything the requirement demands.

whyWrong.A: Cutting the preamble removes compliance-mandated content to solve a problem caching solves without losing anything, and none of it may legally be dropped.
whyWrong.C: An extra model call sounds like a sophisticated compression step, but it adds its own full invocation cost and latency and degrades policy precision.

t1Clause: the preamble is compliance-mandated — invert so the removed sections are unrequired boilerplate rather than compliance content
lessonKey: caching content enable first if order prompt reject removed required sections static

stem: A document-classification pipeline processes 400,000 records weekly. The quality team reviews every customer complaint and every classifier-flagged output, but never samples outputs scored high-confidence. Which addition closes the monitoring gap?

opts.t: Add per-segment breakdowns to the existing weekly dashboard.
Raise the confidence classifier's threshold so fewer records qualify as high-confidence.
Add stratified sampling of the high-confidence stream, across segments and verdict classes.
Rely on the existing complaint and flagged-output reviews as sufficient coverage.

whyRight: The unsampled high-confidence stream is exactly where a novel error pattern first appears, since it never reaches a human through a complaint or a flag. Stratified sampling across segments and verdict classes gives the quality team visibility into that stream instead of waiting for a complaint.

whyWrong.A: Per-segment dashboard breakdowns fix aggregate masking on data already collected; they add nothing for records that were never sampled in the first place.
whyWrong.B: Narrowing the high-confidence label shrinks the unreviewed population without validating any of the records still inside it, leaving the same blind spot smaller but unmeasured.
whyWrong.D: The stem's own gap is that high-confidence records are never sampled, so complaints and flags cannot already cover error types that surface only in that unreviewed stream.

t1Clause: The stem states the pipeline 'never samples' the high-confidence stream; invert to 'already stratifies sampling across the high-confidence stream but the weekly dashboard reports only an aggregate average,' and per-segment breakdowns becomes the fix.
lessonKey: add confidence high sampling stratified stream

stem: A multi-tenant billing assistant must never state another customer's account identifier in a reply, and the compliance officer requires this metric defined before sign-off. Which threshold should the team set?

opts.t: A deterministic pattern or field scan enforced as a hard zero — 0 occurrences per N replies.
Re-anchor the bar to a small non-zero rate, such as fewer than 0.1% of 10,000 replies.
Calibrate the pass bar once a full month of baseline reply volume has been observed.
Log every reply and flag any that mention another customer's account number for review afterward.

whyRight: The requirement is exact and machine-checkable — a specific customer's account identifier either appears in the text or it does not. Code can enforce that boundary precisely, so the metric is a deterministic hard zero measured per N replies, not a rate description chosen after results arrive.

whyWrong.B: This re-anchoring move belongs to an open-ended, model-judged property; this requirement is exact and code-checkable, so a non-zero statistical rate weakens an enforceable boundary into a tolerance.
whyWrong.C: Waiting for baseline volume turns the bar into a description of whatever the system already does, and a deterministic property needs no baseline to define its threshold.
whyWrong.D: Flagging after emission only detects a violation that has already reached the customer; the requirement calls for a hard zero enforced before the reply ships, not a review queue afterward.

t1Clause: The requirement is deterministically checkable ('must never state another customer's account identifier'); invert to an open-ended, model-judged property (e.g., reply tone) proposed at a 0% bar, and re-anchoring to a small non-zero rate becomes the fix.

stem: A coding assistant generates candidate functions behind a test harness that automatically reruns generation up to five times until the tests pass, before any code reaches a reviewer. Which aggregation should the engineering lead adopt to report reliability?

opts.t: `pass@k` — credit the harness for reachable success across the up-to-five attempts.
`pass^k` = 1.0 applied to every attempt, since each rerun is treated as customer-visible.
`pass^k`, since five attempts is a large enough sample to detect hidden instability.
Skip aggregation and rely on the reviewer, since every generated candidate already reaches human review.

whyRight: The test harness catches and reruns failing attempts before any output is exposed, so what matters is whether a passing candidate is reachable within the attempt budget. `pass@k` measures exactly that; the harness's own retries make individual-attempt reliability irrelevant to what the reviewer eventually sees.

whyWrong.B: Demanding a perfect first attempt across five retries ignores that the harness absorbs failures; this bar belongs to steps where a single silent failure reaches the world.
whyWrong.C: Attempt count measures how many times something was tried, not whether a failure is absorbed or exposed; that distinction, not the number five, decides the aggregation.
whyWrong.D: The stem places the harness before the reviewer stage, so only candidates that already passed the tests are ever seen; the reviewer never observes the failed attempts this option assumes.

t1Clause: The harness 'automatically reruns... before any code reaches a reviewer'; invert so every generated candidate deploys directly without passing through the harness, and pass^k becomes the correct aggregation.

stem: A contract-review assistant fabricates clause numbers only for contracts uploaded in the past week; older contracts are still handled correctly. The legal-ops lead wants this fixed before next week's compliance audit. What should the team check first?

opts.t: Move to a higher-capability model, since fabricated clause numbers signal a reasoning limitation.
Add an explicit system-prompt instruction not to state clause numbers it cannot verify.
Expand the evaluation set with more contract examples to measure the fabrication rate precisely.
Check how the newly uploaded contracts were chunked and indexed, since the failure is confined to that recent batch.

whyRight: The failure is confined to one recent batch of documents while everything else still works, which is the data-coverage and chunking signature, not a model deficiency. Checking how the new contracts were chunked and indexed tests the layer the symptom actually points to, before any model change is considered.

whyWrong.A: Fabrication confined to one recent batch is a data-layer signature, not a reasoning limitation; swapping models replaces a component the symptom never implicates.
whyWrong.B: An instruction not to overstate certainty treats the symptom, not the cause, and cannot conjure a clause number that was never correctly indexed in the first place.
whyWrong.C: A larger evaluation set would measure the fabrication rate more precisely without diagnosing which layer produces it, leaving the actual defect unaddressed before next week's audit.

t1Clause: The fabrication is 'confined to contracts uploaded in the past week'; invert to failure occurring broadly and uniformly with retrieval and chunking already verified clean, and moving to a higher-capability model becomes the fix.

stem: An agent pipeline has a p95 latency budget of 3 seconds and is currently averaging 4.1 seconds; no stage-level timing has been collected. Which action should the team take before changing anything?

opts.t: Enable prompt caching on the static portions of every request immediately.
Profile stage-level timing first to identify which stage dominates the overage.
Route routine requests to a smaller cascade model to cut generation time.
Reduce the retrieved passages sent to the model, since retrieval is clearly the slowest stage.

whyRight: Halving a stage that accounts for only a fraction of the total budget barely moves the aggregate number, so the first move is to measure which stage actually owns the 1.1-second overage. Every optimization lever below is real, but none of them is targeted until that measurement exists.

whyWrong.A: Caching is a real lever with no quality cost, but committing to it before profiling assumes the static preamble is the dominant stage, which the stem never establishes.
whyWrong.C: Cascade routing is a genuine lever elsewhere, but its trigger must be validated per segment; applying it before profiling assumes generation is the dominant stage without evidence.
whyWrong.D: The stem states no stage-level timing exists yet, which directly contradicts the claim that retrieval is clearly the slowest stage.

t1Clause: The stem states 'no stage-level timing has been collected'; invert to timing already showing the static preamble dominates the budget, and enabling prompt caching becomes the fix.
